## What you will make

This guide takes you from a table of assumed causal relationships to a labelled
figure that you can save for a manuscript. You only need basic R: no knowledge
of igraph or manual node coordinates is required.

Our illustrative question is whether smoking affects lung cancer, possibly
through tar deposits in the lung. We assume that socioeconomic background
affects both smoking and lung cancer. These are teaching assumptions, not findings
about the real world. A DAG records the relationships you posit; metrodag
chooses where to draw the variables and arrows.

## Install and load the package

Install the development version from GitHub. Include `build_vignettes = TRUE`
if you want these guides available through R's `vignette()` interface; building
them also requires knitr, rmarkdown, and Pandoc.

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes") # Once, if needed
remotes::install_github("hdbt/metrodag")

# Optional: install with locally browsable guides
# install.packages(c("knitr", "rmarkdown"))
# remotes::install_github("hdbt/metrodag", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

```{r load}
library(metrodag)
```

## 1. Write down the arrows

Each row is one arrow, from the variable in `from` to the variable in `to`.
Use short, stable identifiers in this table. You will add readable labels later.

```{r edges}
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("C", "C", "X", "X", "M"),
  to   = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y")
)
edges
```

Here `C` denotes socioeconomic background, `X` cigarettes per day, `M` tar
deposits, and `Y` lung cancer. `C -> X` and `C -> Y` encode a possible common cause
of smoking and lung cancer. `X -> M -> Y` represents the proposed mediated pathway;
`X -> Y` allows a pathway that does not pass through `M`.

Arrows specify direction, not effect size or sign. Missing arrows are also
substantive assumptions. The graph must be directed and acyclic: feedback over
time needs distinct variables for the different occasions.

## 2. Draw the graph

```{r first-dag, fig.cap="The assumed graph, initially drawn using its short variable identifiers.", fig.alt="Four-node DAG: C points to X and Y; X points to M and Y; M points to Y."}
p <- metro_dag(edges)
p
```

Layout and edge routing happen automatically. `metro_dag()` returns a ggplot
object; printing it renders the diagram at the current device size. Lines can
cross or share part of a route: only a station marker represents a variable,
and only the supplied arrow endpoints define relationships.

## 3. Add readable names and the research target

```{r labelled-dag, fig.cap="The same graph with readable labels and an explicit exposure and outcome.", fig.alt="The graph labels C as socioeconomic background, X as cigarettes per day, M as tar deposits, and Y as lung cancer. X and Y have filled role markers."}
display_labels <- c(
  C = "Socioeconomic background",
  X = "Cigarettes per day",
  M = "Tar deposits",
  Y = "Lung cancer"
)

p <- metro_dag(
  edges,
  labels = display_labels,
  exposure = "X",
  outcome = "Y"
)
p
```

The names of `display_labels` match the identifiers in `edges`. Changing a
display label does not rename the variable. Arguments such as `exposure`,
`outcome`, and `adjusted` always use identifiers, so write `exposure = "X"`,
not `exposure = "Cigarettes per day"`.

The filled exposure and outcome markers describe your chosen research target.
An ordinary hollow circle denotes an observed variable without another selected
role. It does not mean the variable is irrelevant. In particular, `M` does not
need a special mediator marker: its proposed position in the graph is visible
from the arrows. Adjustment annotations and unobserved variables are covered in
[Variables, adjustment sets, and analysis views](analysis-views.html).

## 4. Check and save the figure

Check the size and format you intend to export. Width is in millimetres by
default; 180 mm is an example two-column width, not a universal journal rule.

```{r diagnose}
report <- diagnose_metro_dag(p, width = 180, device = "pdf")
report
report$issues
```

`report$ok` is `FALSE` if a rendering error is detected. Warnings still need
inspection even when it is `TRUE`. This checks the drawing, not the causal
assumptions or the appropriateness of an adjustment set.

The following exports actually run when this guide is built. They use a
temporary directory so trying the example will not overwrite your own figures.

```{r export}
figure_dir <- tempdir()
save_metro_dag("smoking.pdf", p, path = figure_dir, width = 180)
save_metro_dag("smoking.svg", p, path = figure_dir, width = 180)
save_metro_dag("smoking.png", p, path = figure_dir, width = 180, dpi = 300)
```

For your project, create a permanent directory and pass its name as `path`:

```{r project-export, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
save_metro_dag("smoking.pdf", p, path = "figures", width = 180)
```

PDF and SVG retain vector lines and text. PNG is a raster image; its resolution
depends on `dpi`. The export function chooses a height if you omit it and
recalculates labels on the export device. Always inspect the saved file at its
intended printed size. See [Preparing figures for publication](publication.html)
for dimensions, fonts, alternative styles, and troubleshooting.

## Already have a graph?

You can enter the same graph in several ways:

| Your starting point | Input to `metro_dag()` |
|:--|:--|
| An edge table | A data frame with `from` and `to` columns |
| An edge matrix | A two-column matrix of variable identifiers |
| Separate node and edge tables | Construct the graph with `metro_graph(nodes, edges)` |
| A named binary adjacency matrix | Construct the graph with `metro_graph_from_adjacency(adjacency)` |
| An igraph graph | A directed, simple, acyclic `igraph` object |
| A tidygraph graph | A directed acyclic `tbl_graph`, in either active context |
| A DAGitty model | A `dagitty` DAG with directed edges and supported node statuses |
| A ggdag model | A `tidy_dagitty` object whose plotting data agrees with its embedded DAG |
| A diagram you want to reuse | The `metrodag_layout` stored on an existing plot |

For example, this uses igraph without changing the graph's causal structure:

```{r igraph-input}
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)
from_igraph <- metro_dag(g, labels = display_labels,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y")
```

An edge list cannot declare a variable that has no arrows. Use a node table to
retain isolated variables and display metadata:

```{r node-table}
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = c("C", "X", "M", "Y", "I"),
  label = c(unname(display_labels[c("C", "X", "M", "Y")]), "Isolated variable")
)
with_isolate <- metro_graph(nodes, edges)
```

The returned graph works with `metro_dag()` and the other graph entry points.
An adjacency matrix must use the explicit `metro_graph_from_adjacency()`
constructor: a matrix passed directly to `metro_dag()` is always interpreted as
a two-column edge list, including a 2 by 2 matrix. In an adjacency matrix,
row A, column B equal to 1 means `A -> B`; rows and columns must name the same
variables, and weights other than 0 or 1 are unsupported.

DAGitty and ggdag inputs require their optional packages. Their original
coordinates are replaced with metrodag's layout. See the import example and
supported statuses in the [analysis guide](analysis-views.html#starting-from-dagitty).
Inconsistent ggdag plotting data and embedded graph metadata are rejected;
converting a plotting table alone would discard causal information.

- [Preparing figures for publication](publication.html): tailor labels, styles,
